sections.html: Botia histrionica (Blyth 1860) is sold in the hobby as the "Golden (Gold) Zebra Loach" and is sometimes called the Burmese Loach. The maximum size is slightly above 10 cm. It has a short nose, a convex head and 5 wide black bands (sometimes irregular and tending to split with age) that disappear towards the bottom of the body. The bands extend into the caudal fin as 2 or 3 vertical stripes on both lobes. A thinner black line runs through the eye, and a smaller line runs from the eye to the mouth; these help distinguish juveniles from the similar-looking young of Botia rostrata and Botia almorhae.
Collected in the Salween Basin of India, China and Myanmar (Burma).

In the author's opinion this is one of the most fearless and active Botia species in the hobby. It is active during the day and is often found swimming freely in the middle of the tank, competing to some extent with relentless swimmers such as barbs.

Botia histrionica is generally very peaceful and social. A community tank with other loaches at the bottom and various barbs in the middle, well planted, with shelters made of coconut shells, driftwood or bamboo pipe pieces and a couple of oval stones, suits it well. The species usually does not make frequent use of hideouts and rests in open areas if undisturbed.

In the author's 200-litre "Indian species tank", four big Botia histrionica are kept with Botia dario (5), Botia striata (5), Botia rostrata (7), Botia almorhae (2), Syncrossus beauforti (1), Syncrossus hymenophysa (2) and a shoal of Puntius arulius (10), Puntius filamentosus (10) and Puntius pentazona (13). They have lived together for a long time without problems, although hierarchy is usually set by size and strength, with bigger specimens ranking higher.

In one smaller tank, two young specimens fought heavily for unknown reasons. The weaker fish was repeatedly hit in the same area, changed coloration completely (probably due to deep stress), and showed a dark blackish spot where it was struck, likely from the other fish's suborbital spines. A similar effect was once seen in Yasuhikotakia eos. This has no long-lasting harmful effect and is extremely rarely seen with proper tank and fish maintenance.

Juveniles show single black blotches on the tips of the dorsal and pectoral fins, subtle black dots at the base of the pelvic and anal fins, and single triangular markers on the caudal fin lobes. Differences in the band shape are already visible at this stage.

Fish photographed in early January 2002 were about 3 months old and 3 cm long. Later they measured 6–8 cm, and one-year-old specimens are likely to approach 10 cm. This growth rate is not often seen in other Botia species, but it depends on environmental conditions; in smaller, less spacious tanks growth is significantly slower.

The golden luster of juveniles steadily disappears as the fish mature. The author notes it is almost impossible to find two identical specimens, as the shape and thickness of the black stripes differ from fish to fish. At around one year old (10 cm), the lighter areas between the stripes retain remnants of golden luster but become increasingly grayish, and additional markings develop on the pectoral and caudal fins. At this stage the fish is easily recognised among other Botia.
